title: The turning of the qiblah
hookLine: during a prayer the direction turns from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:144)

cards: A small mosque on the edge of Medina. A row of men are in the middle of the afternoon prayer, facing north, toward Jerusalem, the way Muslims have prayed for years. Someone comes to the door.
He's just prayed with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and he calls out: the direction has changed. We've been told to face the Ka'ba in Mecca. And the whole row, without breaking the prayer, turns around.
North to south. Their backs are now where their faces were. A mosque in Medina today carries a name that remembers it: the mosque of the two qiblahs.

teach.b: The qiblah is the direction Muslims face in prayer.
For the first years, including about sixteen or seventeen months in Medina, Sahih al-Bukhari says, the Prophet and his companions prayed toward Jerusalem, toward the holy house there.
Commentators connect it with the long line of prophets before him, Abraham, Moses, David, Jesus, whom Muslims count as prophets too.
But the hadith says he longed to face the Ka'ba, the house the Qur'an says Abraham and Ishmael raised. The Qur'an describes him turning his face to the sky.

teach.h: TURN YOUR FACE TO THE SACRED MOSQUE.
teach.b: Then the verse came, in al-Baqarah: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Some people objected. Why change?

teach.h: EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an's answer, two verses earlier, in Pickthall's words: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West." Muslim teachers draw the lesson plainly: the direction was never where God is.

The qiblah is where the community faces, together, so people in every place line up toward one point. The next verse adds that the change was also a test: would people follow, even when it was hard to understand?
Some followed in the middle of a prayer.

teach.h: NOT ONLY WHICH WAY YOU FACE.
teach.b: And elsewhere the Qur'an itself says goodness isn't just turning your face east or west, but faith and generosity and keeping your word.
The direction matters. It was never the whole thing.

how: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca for each prayer, finding the direction by mosque niches, compasses or phone apps, and the mosque of the two qiblahs in Medina is visited by many pilgrims.

games.q: you're in the middle of a prayer, facing Jerusalem. a man at the door calls out that the qiblah has changed to Mecca. what do you do?
o: stop praying and go find out.
games.why: the row turned around without breaking the prayer. the mosque where it's remembered is called the mosque of the two qiblahs.

practice: If you know the direction of Mecca, or can find it on your phone, turn and face it, sitting or standing; people praying anywhere on earth face this same point from every side, like the spokes of a wheel.
If you don't know it, turn slowly in a full circle and recall the verse: unto Allah belong the East and the West. Then sit, facing that way.

wordCard.voice: Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: changed from Jerusalem to the Ka'ba in Mecca, remembered as a row turning mid-prayer.

orig.note: Arabic: the direction faced in prayer. from q-b-l, to face, to meet.

carryVoice: Your line: turn your face. A whole row turned, and kept praying. See you tomorrow.
